utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning, everybody. This is the Pre-Defence conference. I hope we all have a copy of the agenda. We just have to look at the filings that have been made by the Defence. Mr. Milovancevic, just by way of introduction, can I just ask a question? I see that only a few witnesses are mentioned by name. Is there any reason why the rest are not?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can you hold on? I get no interpretation coming through.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can you hear the English?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, I can hear English. Can you start all over again, Mr. Milovancevic? Otherwise it's all lost.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Yes, indeed, we mention the names of just a few witnesses, and the reason for that is that the Defence, when it compiled the witness list, did not have the possibility of conducting proofing sessions with the witnesses. These are individuals who mostly, and the majority of them are from the Republic of Srpska Krajina, there are warrants out for them issued by the Croatian authorities, some of them have long prison sentences up to them, and they fear for their safety, both here and on the way to the Tribunal. So the Defence quite simply, before talking and interviewing the witnesses, could not assess in the proper way of which of these concerns that these people have are realistic and well founded, but will do so as soon as possible, Your Honour, once we have a chance to talk to these people and after we have the recess -- or during the recess we will be able to contact those witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much, Mr. Milovancevic. Mr. Whiting, do you have anything to say?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I certainly do, Your Honour. I'm quite taken aback by this course of action that the Defence has taken on. I have to say that it's -- the Defence is trying to accomplish indirectly what it failed to accomplish directly; that is, it was trying to -- repeatedly tried to postpone the start of the Defence case, trying to buy more time, and when it was -- when this was refused repeatedly by the Trial Chamber, what the Defence has done is it has now failed to comply with the Rules, and it is simply indirectly trying to gain more time, trying to postpone the start of the Defence case, trying to prejudice the Prosecution in its preparation of -- in its preparation to deal and respond to the Defence case. This is -- it's unprecedented, it's improper. And it's quite appalling, in our view. The -- what's not clear to me from what Mr. Milovancevic has said this morning is if any of these individuals have actually agreed to be witnesses. If they have not agreed to be witnesses, they are not witnesses and they shouldn't be on the list and the list then is comprised of the six named individuals. And to be clear here, just so the numbers are on the record, there are 53 witnesses on the Defence list. 47 of them are anonymous. We have the names of only six witnesses. The -- if the witnesses have been contacted and have agreed to be witnesses, then they are witnesses and we should know who they are. There is no -- there is nothing in what Mr. Milovancevic has said, nothing, to justify not providing the names to the Prosecution. There is nothing. We will not -- we -- this can be done confidentially. We are not suggesting that the names should be public, but there is nothing he has said, whether they have agreed to be witnesses, whether they have these fears about coming to the Tribunal, whether they are not witnesses. We should be entitled today to have their names. Because we were supposed to have their names two days ago. So it's already two days late. And we should have the names today, and in any event, this issue must, in our view, be resolved before the recess. This is not -- we cannot go into the recess without knowing who the Defence witnesses are in this case. It tremendously prejudices the Prosecution in its preparation. It will no doubt result in significant delays once we start up again because the Prosecution, in our view, will have a strong basis for delaying the cross-examinations of witnesses because it will have been prejudiced and not have been able to prepare. If I could contrast, just briefly, the approach that the Prosecution took to this issue of delayed disclosure to the approach that the Defence has taken, the Prosecution filed its 65 ter list of witnesses on the 7th of May 2004. On that list were 74 witnesses. Prior to filing the list - prior - the Prosecution sought delayed disclosure for three witnesses, three out of 74. And this was granted. Later, on the 19th of July, 2005, the Prosecution sought to add five witnesses to its list and at the same time, simultaneously, sought delayed disclosure for one of the five. So in total, out of 79 witnesses, the Prosecution sought delayed disclosure for four witnesses. This was at a time, I should say, when the start of the trial was not even scheduled, and was likely to be months if not years away, and in fact, when the Prosecution sought delayed disclosure for the first three witnesses, that was two years before the trial ultimately began. That is in stark contrast to the situation here. Here, the Defence is seeking to delay disclosure of 47 out of 53 witnesses. And it's seeking to do so in a context when the Defence case is to start four days from now. So at most, the Defence -- the Defence somehow has to justify why it cannot disclose to the Prosecution today, but somehow it could disclose in a few weeks or in a month, and there is no possible justification for that. Moreover, if you look at the relevant law about delayed disclosure which has been set out by this Trial Chamber in its decision in the Prosecution's motion, in its decision of the 9th of December, 2005, delayed disclosure is justified only in extraordinary circumstances. It's impossible to believe that there are -- that extraordinary circumstances exist with respect to giving the names to the Prosecution, or that they could possibly exist for 47 out of 53 witnesses. The Trial Chamber - this Trial Chamber - in its decision laid out three factors to consider: The likelihood that the witness would be interfered with or intimidated if the identity of the witness were made known to the Defence and the accused was in the context of a Prosecution motion. In this case, there is absolutely no risk that the witnesses, if disclosed to the Prosecution, would be intimidated or interfered with by the Prosecution. There is simply no basis for such an assertion. Secondly, the extent to which protective measures are necessary not just for the individual case but for future cases. That's inapplicable to this case. And third, the length of time before trial in which the identity of the victims and witnesses must be disclosed. And here again, I think that factor weighs strongly in favour of immediate disclosure because we are four days before the Defence case. The fundamental bottom line is that the Defence has not made -- has not shown why it cannot disclose these names to the Prosecution, why it would in any way threaten the safety of these witnesses, which it just absolutely will not. And this has never ever been done before. It's been tried once, to our knowledge. In the Oric case, the Defence listed 74 witnesses and asked for delayed disclosure of five. It later dropped one of them, so it was delayed disclosure of four of the 74, a far different proportion than what the Defence is seeking here, and the Trial Chamber denied it. Trial Chamber held that the reasons brought forward by the Defence in support of the request for delayed disclosure of the names of the four witnesses are unconvincing and unacceptable. The same is true here. The Defence has not put forward any reason. We would strongly urge, Your Honours, that the Defence be ordered to provide the names of the witnesses today or forgo those witnesses on its list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, any reply?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. All the witnesses on the list have been interviewed and they have agreed to come in and testify and we can give the Prosecution a list of all those names if the Trial Chamber so orders. What is terrible is what my colleague has just said. To say that we are obstructing the Tribunal, to say that we are not respecting the Tribunal, without asking and first consulting the Defence to learn what all that was about, is unbelievable, as far as I can see and I'm concerned. My learned friend of the Prosecution says there are no extraneous circumstances which justify the witnesses' concern. Your Honour, in the information media, a piece of information was published according to which the Croatian secret services have penetrated the Tribunal and are controlling the Tribunal. So people fear for their lives. They fear for their freedom. So that is something that you can read about in the information media. So when people hear things like that, I can't tell them whether it's serious -- a serious threat or not a serious threat. But at any rate, the Defence, when it comes to deliberate about protective measures for the witnesses, will have to talk to the witnesses. That's what I talked about. So for those witnesses for which we consider that protective measures should be put in place, we will talk to them, see whether their demands are realistic and, depending on the results of that interview, will propose or not propose protective measures. But to do away with any doubts about the work of the Defence, we will supply the names of all the witnesses before the day ends. And let me say one more thing: My learned colleague of the Prosecution says that on the 7th of May, 2004, he provided a list of witnesses, and that on the 19th of July, 2005, he asked for an extension. So that is the problem, Your Honour, because my colleague had from March to the 7th of May, 2004, to make up a list, whereas we just had seven days, after being at trial, and without the possibility of going to Belgrade to talk to the witnesses. So we did what we could. We had to makeshift in order to adhere to the deadlines which are not feasible for us. But that is the reason. It wasn't that we were attempting to obstruct the Tribunal and out of a lack of respect for the Tribunal. If the Prosecution wants to win his case by hurling accusations of that kind, I don't think he's going to succeed there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You have made a very telling statement about the Tribunal, which I would like you to substantiate. If you are able to give proof of that, can you give us the proof of this Croatian secret service that penetrated the Tribunal and is controlling the Tribunal? Show us how it did that and how it does control the Tribunal. Secondly, I want to say to you, if you had only seven days to have your witness list, then you are doing a disservice to Mr. Martic and he needs to know that. You were given instructions to defend Mr. Martic some time ago, not seven days ago. I repeat what I said at the last sitting of the Chamber: That you got instructions -- I beg your pardon. You're supposed to have started preparations from the day you got instructions. From that day, you must have sought who your witnesses are going to be, interviewed them, and as you rightly say today, you have interviewed these witnesses that you have listed on your list, and yet you have just told us that you have not been to Belgrade since the last session. So you have not interviewed them in the last seven days. You have interviewed them much earlier. So I will not accept any statement that you have had only seven days. You are at every minute, every opportunity, trying to find space to say you are being prejudiced in this case by the Bench, and this Bench is not prepared to accept that. That you must know and know very clearly. If you haven't prepared your defence, then it's about time Mr. Martic did something about it. But I will not accept that you have not been given time to prepare your case for the Defence. You don't begin to prepare a case for the Defence only at the close of the Prosecution case. You prepare your case from day 1 and you continually adjust according to how things pan out in the trial. Now, if as is clear from what you say, you have interviewed these witnesses, and obviously not in the last seven days, it is -- and you say that, in fact, some of them fear for their lives coming to testify, fear for their lives travelling here, it is surprising that you have not made any application for protective measures up until this time. And the question is: If you are going to need such protective measures, when are you going to make such applications and when is that application going to be granted for those witnesses to be on time to testify when you do know that, by order of this Chamber, you are supposed to start testifying -- leading evidence next week.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, of course I do know, and we shall begin on time. There is nothing contentious about that. I don't think you understood me properly. I was just responding to the Prosecution's assertions that he did everything on time, within deadlines. I didn't broach any new subject, I just tried to indicate the realistic positions that the Defence were facing. And that is why the opposite side is attacking us. But we shall begin on the date you told us to begin. The witness will appear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: In any case, then I'm just -- the Bench is just telling you that what you call realistic is completely unrealistic because you have not had seven days only to prepare. Now on this point of names of witnesses, the Defence is ordered to provide the Prosecution with a full list of the witnesses they intend to call by 15 minutes after the end of this session. Okay? That disposes of that item.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise but, yes, we shall do that straight away afterwards, but don't give us a 15-minute deadline, please. We have to type it out, get the names straight. We have all this but it takes time for us to leave the courtroom, reach the Defence room. We'll need more than 15 minutes. Can we say one hour? But I assume we'll get through it before the hour is out but it's just the technical feasibilities of printing out something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You are supposed to have it ready, Mr. Milovancevic. Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we handed in that list, and said what the witnesses would testify about. All we have to do is to type out the names that we haven't given you which I think -- we think are relevant. So if you want the names, yes, we'll hand the names in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I can go back to your address this morning where you said you could give the list now. And I'm now not saying now, I'm saying 15 minutes after the session. Isn't that generous compared to what you asked for?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, we will abide by your instructions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The question of the estimated time of testimony, let me just find out from you, Mr. Milovancevic, does this -- is this an estimate of the examination-in-chief only or does it include cross-examination and possibly questions by the Bench, and re-examination? The estimate that you have given for each witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this is our approximation, which is always an evaluation of how long the cross-examination -- or examination of witnesses will last or, rather, examination-in-chief and how much time the cross-examination will take and the questions from the Bench, so that's just an assessment, a rough estimate, because we haven't had enough experience in this kind of work, so we looked at the time the Prosecution took and tried to achieve some sort of balance and equivalent time. There might be some 92 bis statements put in too, but at present we were faced with the situation we were faced with, and it is as it stands at present.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The question about 92 bis, I will raise in due course during this conference. What I did want to get clear, and I do appreciate, Mr. Milovancevic, that it is but an approximation, but what I did want to get clarified is whether this is an approximation of both leading, cross, re-exam and possibly also Judges' questions or is it just of leading evidence? I want to assume from what you have said in answer that you tried to estimate leading, cross, re-examination, and questions from the Bench. I thank you for that. Do you have anything to raise on the content of the summaries?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Such as it is, yes, Your Honour, I certainly do have something to raise about that, thank you. Your Honour, in our view, the 65 ter summaries that have been provided to the Prosecution are utterly, utterly inadequate and fail to comply with the Rule. The Rule, as Your Honours know, require the Defence to provide a summary -- "a summary of the facts on which each witness will testify." It is the same requirement for the Prosecution as it is for the Defence. The same language. Though I would note that the Prosecution, in addition to providing a 65 ter summary of its witnesses, is also required to provide prior statements of the witnesses, which, of course, can amplify and explain and make clear what the witness is going to testify about. That -- the Defence does not have that requirement. It is not required to provide to the Prosecution statements it has taken from Defence witnesses. In our view, this makes it all the more important that the 65 ter summaries, which are the only notice that are provided to the Bench and to the Prosecution about what the witness is going to say, that it be in compliance with the Rule. It's all the more important in this case. In our view, the 65 ter summaries that have been provided to the Prosecution are virtually devoid of facts. There are no facts in these summaries. What there are are topics, topics about what the witnesses will testify about. For example, let's look at the first one, MM-084. It says in the 65 ter summary that he will testify about the following facts, but then no facts follow. There are topics that follow. Topic headings. For example, the Vance Plan. He will testify about the Vance Plan. That is not a fact. That is a topic. We don't know what he will say about the Vance Plan, what his evidence will be, what facts he will provide about the Vance Plan. The next witness, MM-085, we are told will testify about "events in Dubica, Cerovljani and Bacin." We are not told what he will say about those events, what facts he will provide, what time period, what events; nothing. In our view, under the jurisprudence of the Tribunal, these summaries are inadequate, and in our view the Defence should be ordered by Monday, we would propose, to provide 65 ter summaries of all its witnesses in compliance with the Rules. With respect to the jurisprudence, I would note that in the Galic case, the Trial Chamber held orally that, "The main purpose of the 65 ter summaries is to give a summary of the facts that enables the other party to prepare for cross-examination." The summaries that have been provided to us fail to do that. They make it impossible to prepare for cross-examination because we do not know what the witness will say, so we cannot prepare to challenge what the witness is going to say. Challenge or accept, perhaps, in some cases, but we cannot prepare cross-examination because we do not know what the witness will say. The Trial Chamber in Galic also noted that it's important to have adequate 65 ter summaries for the Bench to be able to make determinations about the relevance of witnesses before they come, and about the time estimates that have been provided by the Defence, and to judge whether witnesses should be dropped from the list, whether they should be shortened, and so forth. And in this case, there are a number of witnesses about whom the Prosecution has questions about relevance. For example -- but it's impossible to judge for sure, but for example, MM-086, who will testify -- we are told will testify about the mistreatment of Serbs in Zadar. On the face of it, given that information, it's not clear to us what the relevance would be. But without more information, it's impossible really to judge. MM-0109, we are told, will testify about the events before the 19th of August, 1990, and about the proclamation of a state of war through the Knin radio station. Again, without more detail, it's impossible to determine whether that information is really relevant to this trial. Witness MM-118 we are told will testify about events in -- really about Croat crimes. Miljevac alleged Croat crimes, Miljevac Plateau, the Medak pocket, and Maslenica. Again, without more detail, impossible to tell. In the -- just on the subject of more jurisprudence, in the Kupreskic case in 1999, it's a decision of -- I actually have copies of this, if the Court is interested. It's 11th of January, 1999. The Trial Chamber -- the Defence provided inadequate summaries of Defence witnesses and the Trial Chamber found that: "The extremely succinct and summary nature of many Defence witness statements violated the principle of equality of arms since the Prosecution communicated much more detailed Prosecution witness statements to the Defence and to the Trial Chamber before the presentation of its case, thereby enabling the Defence to prepare for cross-examination of Defence witnesses." And in that case, the Trial Chamber ordered that the Defence file more detailed summaries of witness statements. It's unusual for the Prosecution to make an equality of arms argument, but in this case I think it's justified. If the 65 ter summaries that have been provided by the Defence are compared to the 65 ter summaries that were provided by the Prosecution, I can just make a little visual comparison here. These are the Prosecution 65 ter summaries which, again, were in addition to the witness statements provided, so that the Defence had full information about what our witnesses were going to testify about. And this is the Defence summaries. Plainly inadequate. We would ask that they be redone and that they be redone immediately because they should have been done properly Wednesday. We should have had these on Wednesday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Any response, Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, once again, we are not getting --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My learned friend is right when he says these summaries are indeed short -- I apologise. I don't know whether this has anything to do with my mike which has been switched on. These summaries, in other words, are really short and they are certainly not the result of our effort to deprive Prosecution from getting information. We were pressed for time and this is the result of that time pressure that we've had. We heard a suggestion of our learned friend that this should be done by Monday and I would kindly ask the Trial Chamber to grant us a week, until next Monday, because in the meantime we will have our beginning of our trial, preparation of witnesses, we have a lot of work to do, and we are simply talking about the feasibility of things and how to do them. I don't want to -- for us to find ourselves in a situation to face objections that we have not provided enough detail yet again when we provide our summaries.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may make a proposal, my only -- I understand we all have a lot of work to do. I understand the Defence case is beginning next week. I don't want to make unrealistic pressures on the Defence, however my one concern about delaying this too long is that in the event -- we've already got one set of inadequate summaries. In the event the second round are inadequate, we will be a little bit without a remedy because everybody will be on recess by next Friday. So what I would propose is that the Defence file -- provide the Prosecution with a batch, some of the -- some revised 65 ter summaries of, ten, let's say, by Monday or Tuesday of next week and the remainder by Friday of next week. And then that will give us an opportunity to, if we need to, we will have an opportunity to raise objections to the Trial Chamber. That's my only concern. But I'm agreeable to allowing the Defence to have sufficient time to accomplish its task.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, you asked for a week. You asked for a week to give these statements. Did I understand you correctly? Yes, okay. Mr. Whiting, the Chamber has a view on this issue which we would like to share with the parties, and if you agree with it and Mr. Milovancevic agrees, we will make that the order, that by Monday noon the Defence provide the Prosecution with detailed summaries of the witnesses who are going to be called in the week before recess and in the week immediately after recess. And then in a week's time, before we go on recess, they can give the balance of the statements -- of the summaries, detailed summaries. Would that be okay with you? I don't want to order them to make them give you ten by Monday and then those ten are not proper.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That's fine, Your Honour. My only concern on that is that it's my understanding that there will only be one witness next week, and I don't know how many witnesses will be after the recess, but if this amounts to us seeing two summaries, you know, I don't know. It would be nice if we had a few more, but I'm not going to quibble.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Wouldn't you use the time during recess at least to see the rest?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes. As I said, it's not an issue about getting them -- we don't need all of them on Monday. It's just an issue about having an opportunity to raise objections if the ones we get are still inadequate, that's all. But the proposed order is fine, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That would cut down the work load on your side, Mr. Milovancevic, wouldn't it, at least between now and the start of the Defence case. Is that okay?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. We agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: All right. Fine. Then it is so ordered that the Defence shall provide the Prosecution with detailed summaries of witnesses scheduled for the week before the beginning of recess and the week after the beginning of recess. At least for those two weeks, the witnesses scheduled for those two weeks must be given by Monday noon, and by no later than Friday, the 14th of July, the balance of the statements, summaries of the statements, must be given to the Prosecution. Okay? Mr. Milovancevic, Mr. Whiting has raised a number of issues about the statements that you gave. I'm not quite sure whether it is worth us going through the statements now that you are going to give new statements. It's probably not worth it -- new summaries, rather. Thanks, Judge. We will have to look at your new summaries when we next see them. There are a few things we still need to sort out. When -- by when, Mr. Milovancevic, do you think or -- let me take a step back. Is it anticipated that any of the Defence witnesses are going to require protective measures? And if so, by when can we expect applications for such protective measures?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, according to the information that the Defence has available at the moment, it seems to us that a lot of witnesses will seek protective measures. What is important at this moment is that not for a single moment these protective measures will be used to gain time or to seek delay in the testimonies of these witnesses. We will seek protective measures in due course, we will explain why we are seeking them, and we will provide the Trial Chamber with a list of witnesses who seek protective measures. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] You just mentioned the name of a witness who you say was a protected witness and he's going to seek protective measures. May that name please be deleted. I do see that it doesn't appear on the transcript. If it can just stay like that. Mr. Milovancevic, what the Trial Chamber would appreciate, if it's possible, and it would expedite the proceedings, is if you could determine all the witnesses that you think will require protective measures and just put them in one motion. That would be very helpful in that -- then we don't have to deal with many motions as we go along.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we believe that this is agreeable and we will act in accordance with your instruction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may? According to our information, the witness that the Defence referred to - I won't use his name out of an abundance of caution - but did not testify with protective measures in the Milosevic case. It was in open session and his name was used, but maybe there has been an understanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's okay. Again out of an abundance of caution, let's just leave it as if it was protective measures. We'll see later when we have got the full truth about it. If I may just go back to the summaries, am I right to say that the detailed summaries that are going to be filed, they will also be filed with the Chamber? Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Now, there is also the question of -- and you raised it yourself, Mr. Milovancevic, in your -- in one -- in discussing one of the points a little earlier, that some of your witnesses may be 92 bis witnesses. Now, my prima facie, or perhaps the Bench's prima facie view of the summaries that you filed was that a lot of those witnesses could be 92 bis witnesses, because a lot of them corroborate one another. For example, I personally counted 11 witnesses that are testifying on the same topic, political developments, and eight who are testifying on relations between Croats and Serbs. Now, in fact those two topics are so closely related that it could easily be said 19 people are being called to testify on one topic. Now, either some of them could be cut off completely or if they deal with -- if each one of them deals with an extra point which none of the others deals with, at least they could come up via 92 bis. Maybe one of them could be viva voce, but the rest, who are corroborating, could come 92 bis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, due to the brevity of these summaries that we have provided to the Trial Chamber and the Prosecution, one might gain the impression that the 11 witnesses speak about the same topic, the political situation, that is, and the rest about the relationship between the Croats and the Serbs. However, as far as I can tell you at the moment, all of these witnesses also speak about the actions of the accused, and this is the criterion that is crucial, whether a statement can be introduced according to 92 bis Rule. In any case, when we took the witnesses' statements, we made sure that they would not testify about one and the same thing. We just provided the summaries in that way. In any case, we will bear in mind what you've just told us and we'll try and, wherever possible, suggest the use of the Rule 92 bis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, but in any case, you yourself had referred to the possibility of using 92 bis, and I would imagine also that the more detailed summaries that tell us facts that you -- the witnesses are going to testify about will enable us to determine whether 92 bis is appropriate or not. I would just like to deal with some other matters that I think need attention. I think it is important for the Defence to state who is going to testify next week and on the 14th of August. Is that a fair comment, Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, yes, it is a fair comment. Next week we are going to hear one witness whose name I mentioned. He will testify over a long period of time and he will testify about a long period of time. He will testify about important facts, and we believe that we will be able to finish that witness next week, that he will fill up the time until the recess. As for the witness after the recess, since we are in the process of making the detailed list, until the end of the week I would kindly ask to you grant us time to tell you that at the moment when we provide more detailed summaries. It will be easier to do then than at this moment. I don't want to improvise, Your Honours. Whatever I say here is binding upon me and this is my attitude towards what I'm saying in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milovancevic. Mr. Milovancevic, is it possible that any exhibits will be tendered through these witnesses? Because any exhibits that are going to be tendered through these witnesses must also be identified to the Prosecution early.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we have provided the list of evidence that we intend to use. Of course, we will try to introduce that evidence through our witnesses. We are aware of the problem that we are facing at the moment. The same evidence should be part of the e-court. However, due to some problems that have appeared during the trial with regard to the distribution of the material by the Registry that has been pointed out by the Trial Chamber, we have our case manager now and we will try and remove the problem as we go, and I believe this is the problem that the Trial Chamber is pointing to us at the moment. We are aware of the -- our obligation that the evidence that we intend to lead should be part of the electronic system. We will try and translate all of the materials and, when we hear the witnesses, we will make sure that the Trial Chamber and the Prosecution know beforehand what evidence we intend to introduce through each and every one of these witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure we are together. I'm actually talking not necessarily about evidence in general, I'm talking specifically about exhibits. And my question was to you: Are there any exhibits that the Defence intends to tender through the witness that is testifying next week, and the witness that's testifying in the week after recess? And I was saying if there are any exhibits to be tendered through those witnesses, then those exhibits should be identified to the Prosecution and to the Chamber also as early as the identification of the witnesses for this next week and the week after recess, because everybody needs to prepare on those exhibits. Do I come out clearer now? Thank you very much, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Thank you very much. I really was off the point. And I now understand what you have asked me to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And you undertake to provide those exhibits to the Prosecution, together with the detailed summaries of these witnesses for next week and the week before -- I beg your pardon, the week after recess. That being so, it is so ordered. Let me just mention also that the sitting on the 13th, it's being disturbed slightly. We may have to start 20 minutes late, at about 20 past 9.00, because of the swearing-in ceremony of a new Ad Litem Judge who will be arriving and the fact that most judges are not going to be around on that day and those that are around are being urged to attend the ceremony. What I wanted to find out, Mr. Milovancevic, and I don't know whether this is something that is usually disclosed here or not. Where I come from, it's no secret. You've given us 53 witnesses. Can I assume that Mr. Martic is not going to testify? Or is he one of the 53? Or is he going to be a 54th?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we have considered that possibility. Mr. Martic will most probably testify. Most probably Mr. Martic will testify, and he would be the 54th witness on the list. This is the current position of the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And if he does testify, then we need to get an estimate of the length of time he's going to testify for so that we are able to compute the period.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, since the estimate of the duration of the possible testimony by Mr. Martic will depend on the length of the testimony of the witnesses that are already on the list, we will take all that into consideration and in the shortest possible time we will provide the Trial Chamber with our estimate. At this moment, I would not be able to give you any estimate. This will largely depend on our final agreement with Mr. Martic and the topic that he will testify on. I would kindly ask you to take this explanation as a reasonable position of the Defence that will do everything in their power to inform the Trial Chamber of all the details in due course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, I am trying very hard to take this as a reasonable explanation of the Defence, but what I find a little difficult to understand is where you say that the duration of the possible testimony by Mr. Martic will depend on the length of the testimony of the witnesses that are already on the list, I don't know how that can depend on -- how those two can be interdependent. Mr. Martic -- I would have imagined in fact that Mr. Martic would be, if you are going to call him, he would be the one witness that would take the longest time because he's got to deal with all the counts and all the facts, and you just give an estimate of how long you think he will stay in the box for, and I don't know how that depends on the people on the list. And I understand that you may not have taken a final decision whether you are going to call him or not, but if you do call him, you need to make that decision very soon, because if you are going to call him, we need to factor into the time estimated for the Defence case the time that Mr. Martic is going to spend testifying. And you see, one thing that we needed to resolve today, and we are not going to be able to resolve, and this is causing a delay, is whether or not the hours that you estimate - you've estimated 300 hours, which is four and a half months - whether those are justified and whether those should be the hours that the Defence should be allocated. We have already indicated -- you have already indicated that some of the witnesses indeed may come 92 bis and that may cut down on a lot of hours, but if Mr. Martic is going to testify, then that may increase your hours, and other people outside this courtroom require this estimate for administrative purposes. And we are now not able to make this estimate.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, what you have just said is very true. As far as the time is concerned for the witnesses on our list, this is the time that the Prosecution had, and we believe that the Defence should have the opportunity to use up as much time as the Prosecution. As far as Mr. Martic is concerned, and if you are agreeable with that, by the end of next week we will inform you exactly whether Mr. Martic is going to testify, when - I believe this will be at the end of our case if that happens - and how long Mr. Martic will take. Your Honour, we do not expect that Mr. Martic will testify for a month. We don't believe that his testimony will take that much longer than the testimony of other witnesses, and we don't expect that his testimony will have a drastic impact on the duration of the case. In any case, if you will allow us to talk to Mr. Martic and inform you about his testimony after our conversation with our client.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I hear that, Mr. Milovancevic, but you see, end of next week is end of term, and we are not here to work on issues. We need this information before we go on recess. We've got to work on it. As I say, there are other departments in the Tribunal outside just the Chamber who need this information. But also the Chamber needs this information for scheduling purposes. I don't think it should take you that long to sort out with Mr. Martic the question of his testifying. You should be able to do that today sometime and you can tell us on Monday. I mean, this is -- this must be something that has occupied your minds from day 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. We'll do as you have instructed. We will inform you of that on Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Having said that, I just want to say that the issue of the hours allocated to the Defence still remains unresolved. In reply to what you said, Mr. Milovancevic, that you -- the Defence must have the same amount of time as the Prosecution had, I don't think it's correct to say that. It all depends on various factors. It depends on the witnesses, the number of witnesses you have, what they are going to testify about, how they are going to testify, are they mainly 92 bis or are they mainly viva voce, are they all viva voce? And in my view, you could take a little more than the Prosecution or it could take far less than the Defence [sic]. In a situation where you have about 53 witnesses as against 74 that they had, expectations would be that you would probably take less. I think what is important is that the Defence must get an opportunity to present its case and place it on the record, and it must place it effectively. That is the important thing. And unfortunately, in this Tribunal, we have to estimate time because time is needed -- is used for various things, and we are going to have to then postpone the question of time to sometime before we start the Defence case, and hoping that by then we will have resolved all the issues that impact on time. I'm going to suggest that that issue remains postponed to Tuesday, the 11th, when the Defence case begins. Whatever information has to be given relating to the time must be given by Monday, the 10th, Mr. Milovancevic. Then we can deal with it on the 11th. Any outstanding issues that you would like to raise, Mr. Whiting?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Only five, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Five?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes. They are brief, though.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Usually lawyers say one and then they raise five, so I thought I would say five.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And raise one?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: No, it will actually be five. The first is just to note that actually the Prosecution didn't call 74 witnesses. Far fewer than that. And by our estimate we used 260 hours for -- to present the Prosecution case, which is far below what the Defence has proposed. They have proposed 320 hours for the Defence. But having said that, I agree with Your Honour's observation that there is no rigid mathematical equivalence here. It could be more, it could be less, it depends on what the evidence is, but I just wanted to note that. The second is now that we've learned for the first time today that Mr. Martic himself will most likely be a witness, not only do we, in our view, need the estimate of time, but more importantly, we need a 65 ter summary for him. He is a witness like any other, and a 65 ter summary should be prepared and we should have that with the other 65 ter summaries, because knowing the complete Defence case could affect how the Prosecution prepares for cross-examinations of individual witnesses and what issues it deals with and how it prepares for that. So we -- in our submission, we should have a 65 ter summary for Mr. Martic along with the others by the deadline of next Friday. I don't know if I should -- should I continue with all the issues or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you want that resolved before you continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Perhaps we should.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I guess that is -- speaks for itself, Mr. Milovancevic. That is, it can't be otherwise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we still have not made a definite decision with respect to Mr. Martic's testimony. What we know so far is that we think that he should testify, that he would be -- will be testifying. Now, through the list of witnesses, and our introductory address, the Prosecution will gain insight into our Defence case and Mr. Martic, as a witness testifying on his own behalf, will speak about all the facts raised by the Prosecutor and that other witnesses addressed. Now, I should like to ask that more time be left for Mr. Martic's testimony. It will be a detailed testimony, it will relate to an enormous number of facts, and I think that it is in the interests of both the Prosecution and the Trial Chamber to have this presented as best as possible. We see no danger that the Prosecutor will not be able to view the case as a whole, having worked on it for so many years. Of course, the Prosecution has the right to be made aware of the facts of the testimony but we have to adjust ourselves to the situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, I don't know why life is becoming so unnecessarily difficult when it shouldn't be. If you are going to call Mr. Martic as a witness, then he is a witness, then you must give a 65 ter summary of his testimony. It can't be otherwise. And as I said, the question whether or not Mr. Martic is going to testify is a question that should have occupied your mind much earlier than today when the Bench is raising the question. And you should -- it's part of the strategy, and you should be knowing by now. I don't take kindly to your prevarication on whether or not Mr. Martic is going to testify. This is a fundamental decision that you take when you plan your strategy, and for you now to want to delay the proceedings because you have not taken a decision on this is really not acceptable, I must say. I do not think we should delay more than this. It has just actually struck me that it looks like I made an order a little earlier which is making it impossible for us to give an estimate of the Defence period in terms of Rule 75 ter, and we have just been pushed against the wall by all these uncertainties that are coming from the Defence case, you know. I think -- I think, Mr. Milovancevic, if you are going to call Mr. Martic as a witness, by the time that you give the detailed summaries of the witnesses to the Prosecution, you must have a detailed summary of Mr. Martic's testimony. Otherwise, we -- the Bench and the Prosecution will be entitled to assume that the witnesses that you are going to call are the witnesses for whom you have given summaries by the end of next week.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Martic will testify and we'll do our best to provide the summary by next Friday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Whiting?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I was just going to go on to my other matters, if I may. Or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Whiting, I see you want to go on to the next point. My mind at the moment is occupied -- well, when I said 75 ter, I meant 73 ter. The Chamber has to make this estimation pursuant to 73 ter of the period of the Defence phase and I'm trying to work out through my mind whether, if we get this information by next Friday, we will be able to do so, will the Bench be able to do its job before we go on recess? And lest I forget it, can I ask you to hold your four items. Let's resolve this one. Mr. Milovancevic, are you able to venture a suggestion on how to deal with this situation? The Chamber must make a ruling in terms of 73 ter (E) on the Defence case. And for it to be able to do so it must have all the information, all the summaries before. In other words, it must have a proper filing by the Defence in terms of 65 ter (G), and this 65 ter (G) filing is not ready right now. How do we get out of this problem? How do you suggest we get out of this problem? We can take a break and you can answer when we come back, because it looks like Mr. Whiting also has more questions to raise. May I suggest that you apply your mind during the break. Court adjourned, come back at quarter to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just to round up, Mr. Milovancevic, the Chamber has sort of considered the situation, and we make this order, that the final determination of the estimated period of the Defence evidence will be made on the 14th of August. This, however, does not mean that you've got -- the Defence must give us the information we require by then. The information we still require before we go on recess so that we can consider that. Having made that order, the Defence must also understand that because of this delay, there may be delays in processing your payments because all that will not be having the determination until then. Okay, Mr. Milovancevic? You understand that? You may go on to your next points, Mr. Whiting. Yes, Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, yes, I understood you fully. A moment ago, before the break, we asked -- you asked about the duration of Mr. Martic's testimony. The duration of testimony is linked to the overall duration of the Defence case, and we would like to tell you straight away, here and now, that it is the Defence's position that Mr. Martic's testimony should not influence the time stipulated on the list. We'll try and comply with the number of hours that we stipulated on the list. Of course, there might be some witness movement, but at this point in time, that would be our preliminary position. It's, of course, an approximation but I think that it is something that will be of importance to the Trial Chamber and we'll try to stick to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I hear what you say and I appreciate what you say, Mr. Milovancevic. You're missing one point, though. The point is that at some stage the Chamber must make a determination, in terms of Rule 73 ter (E) of the length of time that the Defence will take to present its case. In other words, this means that the estimate -- the 300 hours estimate given by the Defence is not taken as gospel. The Chamber must still make a determination, and that determination can only be made when the Chamber has seen the detailed summaries of the evidence that is going to be presented, and a determination has been made how the hours can be cut down, either by getting some of the witnesses as 92 bis witnesses or cutting some of them completely. So it is not just because of Mr. Martic's testifying or not testifying that we are not able to make this determination. We are not able to make the determination because we must still get this full summary, complete summary, of the testimony to be given by all the witnesses. Okay? I hope that clears the matter. Mr. Whiting, you may go on to the second of your four remaining points.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The good news is we are actually on the third of the -- I've already covered two. We are on number 3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Have you?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I don't know what number 2 was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Number 1 was to tell the Court what the time was that we used, and then number 2 was the 65 ter summary for Mr. Martic. So number 3 now is that the -- with regards to the exhibit list that has been provided by the Defence, Rule 65 ter (G)(ii) requires the Defence -- the last sentence of that Rule is that, "The Defence shall serve on the Prosecutor copies of the exhibits so listed." Now, we have received two lists, exhibit lists, from the Defence. One are exhibits that have ERN numbers. We don't need copies of those. We have those documents. They got them from us. The other list, however, are documents without ERN numbers and for those, we would need copies of the exhibits, and we would ask that the Defence be ordered to provide those copies today to us of those exhibits. This should -- this is again something that should have been done on Wednesday, as part of its compliance with Rule 65 ter (G). It was not done and we would ask that it be done by today so that we have those exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, I'm sure you are aware of that Rule.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I addressed that question in part when I said that the Defence entered this stage under circumstances which meant that we had to hurry up because we have just recently been given a case manager, for objective reasons, and therefore the second list we shall prepare within the shortest space of time, Your Honour. But this was just a physical job that had to be done. So that is why we weren't able to do so thus far. I think that in the coming week, we will have complied and finished the job.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milovancevic. I'm not quite sure -- you obviously have proofed these witnesses and taken statements from them. It's just making a copy and giving it to the opposite side. Why does it become so difficult to do it today?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It doesn't refer to witness statements. It is a description of the documents. Some documents have ERN numbers and we have marked those. Other documents do not have the ERN number, so the Prosecutor can't find them, and we'll have to deal with them, process them, copy them, and send them to the Prosecutor. So in addition to making the summaries for the witnesses who are on the list, this is a very lengthy process, requiring a lot of time. We have done our best to make a list of the documents, to select them, and to put them on the list, and we know that the problem exists. We are fully conscious of that. Of course, during the coming week we'll try and deal with the problem so that we can supply the Prosecution with the material necessary. When the first witness testifies, the Prosecutor will certainly have a list of the material that we wish to introduce through that witness. So those are the circumstances. I can't say any more than that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Whiting?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, by my count, there are only 142 documents that we are seeking, and I'm not sure why it should take a week to copy 142 documents. That should be done -- should be able to be done today and if, at the latest, Monday. I would agree to having them first thing on Monday, but it seems to me that's certainly enough time to copy 142 documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: During the short break, I thought we -- we became aware of a further filing by the Defence which increases the number of exhibits from 262 -- from 120 to 262. I'm not sure whether you have seen that filing, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I do. I have it here in front of me. And this is -- this is -- the first 120 exhibits are ones that have ERN numbers. We do not need copies with those. We are fine with that. We will print out our own copies. That's fine. The second list contains 142 items, and that's what I was referring to. Those are the ones that we need copies of, and I would think that by Monday -- I don't see what the difficulty would be providing us copies of those by Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will do that, Your Honour, yes, we will have it by Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The next point?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The next point has to do with expert witnesses from the Defence. As far as we can tell, there are two experts identified on their list, MM-132 and MM-133. We note that the description -- with respect to MM-132, the Defence has written in their summary that the witness has prepared a written statement in accordance with Rule 94 bis. With respect to MM-133, the Defence writes that the witness will prepare a written statement. So the distinction has been made. We would ask, with respect to the one -- to the expert witness who has prepared the expert report, that that be filed on us, that we be provided a copy immediately of that. Rule 94 bis contemplates -- which deals with expert reports, contemplates a 30-day period after the opposite party receives an expert report for the opposite party to evaluate and consider that report and determine whether they will contest it or not. My concern is that if these aren't acted on soon, we will be facing delays later on. If this report is ready, there is no reason why it can't be provided to us now, triggering the 30-day period for us to evaluate it. I would secondly ask that, with respect to the expert who has not yet prepared the report, according to the Defence, that perhaps we could get some indication of when that might be ready and when that might be filed, keeping in mind this 30-day period that will have to run.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Fair request, Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, certainly. We are aware of 94 bis Rule and the deadlines there. And we shall give the Prosecutor the report as soon as we are physically able to do so. And I'd like to ask my learned friend of the Prosecution to bear the following in mind: We will certainly respect the deadline and leave expert witnesses for a later stage of the Defence case so that the Prosecution will certainly have enough time. All we are dealing with now is the situation as it stands at the moment. So as soon as the first report is accessible to us, as soon as we receive it in The Hague, we will send it over to the Prosecution. It is being prepared as we speak, and we'll do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, if we could just be a little forecast: One, how soon will you be physically able to give the Prosecutor the report? Two: The request is that the 94 bis report that has already been written out be given now, or today sometime, and then the one that still has to be written, give us an estimation of time by when you think it will be given. I hear what you say there, but unfortunately, you are not answering the question, the request, as it came.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the second report, which isn't finished yet, we could hand over immediately after the recess. That second one. The one that is complete, it's being typed out, printed out, and before the weekend, we can't complete the job physically. It has to be ready so that we can receive it and then hand it over to the Prosecution. So would the Trial Chamber please bear that in mind and try and understand the position we are in?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Only if you tell us and you sort of play your cards open with us. Where is it being typed, how long will it take to type? When will it be sent to you? And how long will it take to reach you? You know, if you want the Chamber to take -- to accommodate you, please play open cards with the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, of course it is in our best interests to provide you with facts. The first report that is being printed, that is in the pipeline, is a military expert report. It is finished. The material has been written. But it is now being typed out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Where, where, where?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In Belgrade. And we expect - i.e., I have information - that we should have it by the end of the weekend. This is the situation at hand. This is what we are facing. And the situation with the expert report, the military report, is that it has been drafted, it is being typed out, it is being compiled, it is being marked in the way it should be marked, it is being processed, and that's why we have told you that the report is ready. And the second one is being drafted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before you go to the second one. You say you will have this first one by the end of the weekend. Can we then say that by Monday morning, you can give a copy to the Prosecution? By Monday, the 10th?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I could kindly ask you that this should -- that this isn't on Monday the 10th but Wednesday because that would give us time to do our part of the job, as we should. That material is now in Serbian. It has to be translated. And we now face this technical problem that is connected with the work of other people, not only the expert himself. That's why I am asking for this deadline, which I hope we will be able to meet, the deadline being Wednesday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay, Wednesday the 12th. Okay. The second report, Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That one could be prepared immediately after the recess; i.e., in mid-August.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Why can it not be prepared almost immediately and during the recess, if need be, so that immediately we come from recess, it is discovered to or disclosed to the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I may have not been precise. This is what I meant. Immediately after the recess, we will be able to disclose this material to the Prosecution, and this is what I had in mind. I apologise for the imprecision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. That's the answer finally.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. That's absolutely fine with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Though I would note that in our -- the 30-day time in Rule 94 bis starts to run when we receive an English version of the report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So -- my final point is really a minor one --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before you go to the final point, so it is so ordered, the one will be given on Wednesday the 12th, the first report, and the second report immediately on arrival, that is on the 14th of August. Your final point, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The final point is really just to note that the Bench has emphasised the importance of the Defence, with respect to the next week and the week after, informing the Prosecution of which witnesses will testify, in addition, the exhibits that will be tendered through those witnesses. I assume from that but just wanted to underscore that this is a protocol for the future of the Defence case and that we will always be informed ahead of time with some notice - at least a week, I would think - which witnesses are going to be coming, which -- the next witnesses are going to be coming and which exhibits that will be tendered through those witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I think that goes without saying, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree with that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The final point I would like -- the Bench would like to raise with the parties is just to give you notice that early in the autumn, when we come back from recess, the Chamber would like to provide a scheduling order for the remainder of the trial, and we just mention this just to put you on notice so that you can -- so that you can be able to expect, having been given that scheduling, when to be ready for any rebuttal or rejoinder evidence, final briefs and closing arguments. We will do that as soon as we come back in early autumn, okay?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would just ask if we could -- if the parties could briefly be heard with respect to those issues before the scheduling order is issued, we would be grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If you will remember to ask to be heard at the time, the Chamber is -- at times just becomes forgetful and might go ahead and give an order.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'll remember to raise it after the recess.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. You do that. You're finished on your items. Mr. Milovancevic, do you have any items that you would like us to deal with during this conference that we haven't so far dealt with?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. At this point in time, no, Your Honour. The only thing I would kindly ask for is the precise scheduling for next week, i.e., when the sessions start next week, whether in the morning or in the afternoon. I'm not sure about that so I would kindly ask you to advise me as to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milovancevic. You will certainly be advised of that. We are sitting in the mornings next week, at 9.00. So right through the week. I guess I'm correct?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is that it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Just to remind you again, on the 13th, we are starting 20 minutes late. Court adjourned and we will reconvene on Tuesday, the 11th, at 9.00, in this courtroom. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: at 11.12 a.m., to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 11th of July, 2006, at 9.00 a.m. 20 21 22 23 24 25
